passages.title: Passage 1
passages.instructions:
Questions 1–40

You should spend about 60 minutes on Questions 1–40, which are based on the reading passage below.
passages.body:
Food Deserts and Public Health

A Food deserts describe neighbourhoods with limited access to affordable nutritious groceries, often overlapping low-income areas where supermarkets closed after suburban flight and discriminatory lending practices. Residents rely on convenience stores stocking shelf-stable processed items high in sodium and sugar, contributing to diet-related diseases including hypertension and diabetes. Epidemiologists map access using distance metrics and vehicle ownership, though lived experience includes time poverty when multiple bus transfers carry heavy bags. The author cautions the term can oversimplify structural racism and corporate divestment decisions treating certain districts as unprofitable despite dense populations needing fresh produce. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.

B Nutrition transitions globally replaced traditional staples with ultra-processed foods marketed heavily to children through sponsorship of sports and cartoon mascots. Urban planning that zones large lots for big-box retailers excludes smaller greengrocers while privileging drive-through outlets along arterial roads. Community gardens and farmers markets partially fill gaps yet cannot substitute reliable refrigerated supply chains year-round. Cooperative grocery startups face financing hurdles when banks perceive high theft risk stereotypes, becoming self-fulfilling when underinvestment leads to higher prices forcing residents to shop farther away weekly, spending scarce cash on transit instead of vegetables. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results.

C Health consequences accumulate across lifecourse: childhood obesity tracks into adulthood cardiovascular risk, while pregnant people lacking folate-rich foods face neural tube defect elevations. Clinics integrate dietary counselling yet prescriptions for healthier eating ring hollow without grocery access. Medicaid pilots reimburse nutrition education while stop short of covering produce prescriptions fulfilled at local markets when reimbursement codes lag innovation. Hospital systems screen for food insecurity at intake, referring patients to pantries that struggle with donation volatility and culturally inappropriate baskets ignoring diabetic needs among communities whose cuisines centre rice or tortillas unfairly stigmatised by one-size dietary guidelines.

D Policy tools include tax incentives enticing supermarkets into underserved corridors, mobile markets serving seniors in housing towers, and acceptance of SNAP benefits at online retailers with delivery fees eroding value. Zoning reforms permit corner stores to expand fresh sections if grants fund refrigeration upgrades. School meal standards raise cafeteria quality, sometimes the primary caloric source for students experiencing weekend hunger. Sugar-sweetened beverage taxes fund recreation programmes, though regressivity concerns push designers toward pairing taxes with subsidies for bottled water stations in parks lacking fountains, addressing heat exposure compounding dehydration risks during summer shifts for outdoor workers living in affected districts.

E Retail labour conditions influence community health when understaffed stores reduce stocking of perishables that spoil quickly. Wage theft in food supply chains depresses incomes available for groceries. Immigrant workers in meatpacking plants faced disproportionate infection during pandemics, revealing interconnections between workplace safety and food system resilience. Labor advocates tie fair contracts for warehouse pickers serving e-commerce groceries to ethical consumption campaigns, arguing cheap delivery subsidised by injury rates undermines public health narratives focusing only on consumer choice without supply-chain justice examining who bears risk cultivating and packing food. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results.

F Measurement debates question whether opening one supermarket suffices or community ownership ensures sustained affordability. GIS models sometimes ignore informal vendors selling affordable produce despite lacking permits, leading policymakers to misidentify deserts. Participatory mapping with residents captures night-shift workers relying on closed stores after hours. Food sovereignty movements emphasise culturally appropriate access rather than importing models privileging kale over traditional legumes. The writer urges intersectional analysis linking housing, transportation, and clinic hours rather than isolated nutrition interventions blaming individuals for systemic scarcity engineered by decades of disinvestment and redlining cartographies still shaping credit access today. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

G Looking ahead, the author believes eliminating food deserts requires antiracist economic development, living wages, and planning that treats nourishment as public infrastructure. Telehealth dietitians cannot replace physical availability of affordable ingredients. If retailers continue exit strategies chasing affluent suburbs, health disparities will persist regardless of wellness apps tracking macros. Integrated investments in transit, cooperative stores, and accountable zoning offer a pathway where public health agencies collaborate with housing authorities instead of sermonising about personal responsibility while ignoring empty lots where markets once stood serving grandparents now travelling hours for milk. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.
